title: Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme (CPRS Fuel Credits) Bill 2009 [No. 2]

divisions.question: Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme (CPRS Fuel Credits) Bill 2009 [No. 2] and Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme Amendment (Household Assistance) Bill 2009 [No. 2] - Third Reading - Read a third time

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The coalition argued that the Social Security and Other Legislation Amendment (Income Support for Students) Bill 2009 should be completed before moving to the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme bills, noting the student bill was near finalisation and needed to provide certainty for 2010. The government refused opposition offers to facilitate this, including giving up a matter of public importance, leading the coalition to use procedural measures to delay the CPRS bills.

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The government argued the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme would reduce emissions, create jobs, and drive investment, citing Treasury modelling of 1.7 million jobs by 2020 and $19 billion in renewables; opponents including the Coalition and Greens criticized the bill for risking job losses (e.g., 66,000 in mining), harming trade-exposed industries, and failing to achieve meaningful global emissions reductions without a comprehensive international agreement.

speeches.speaker: Helen Kroger
speeches.brief: The coalition senator argued that the government's Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme is flawed, citing independent Frontier Economics modelling that showed a better alternative achieving a 10% unconditional emissions cut by 2020 with only a 5% rise in household power bills, and warned the scheme would cost jobs, damage key industries, and should be opposed unless significantly amended.

Senator Bob Brown moved an amendment requiring the government to commit to unconditional emissions reductions of at least 25% below 1990 levels by 2020 and a willingness to reach 40% under a global treaty.

speeches.speaker: Kate Lundy
speeches.brief: The Labor government's Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme (CPRS) will reduce Australia's emissions, protect the economy, and create thousands of clean-energy jobs, including through the $1.5 billion Solar Flagships program and the new Capital Wind Farm, which has 67 turbines and will supply 60,000 homes.

Senator Bob Brown moved an amendment requiring the government to enter 2009 climate treaty negotiations with an unconditional commitment to reduce emissions by at least 25% below 1990 levels by 2020, and up to 40% if part of a global treaty.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Parry
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme bills should be called a tax, rejected the legislation as flawed and harmful to jobs and the economy, and claimed the Prime Minister was using the scheme for political purposes rather than genuine climate action. The speaker also questioned climate science, citing hacked emails and scientific dissent, and opposed rushing the bills through Parliament before international climate talks.

speeches.speaker: Scott Ryan
speeches.brief: The speaker argued against the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme bills, stating they would create an irreversible personal property right, act as a hidden tax, threaten electricity generation in Victoria, and fail to meaningfully address climate change while harming the economy; they called for delaying the legislation until after the Copenhagen conference and until other nations take similar action.

Senator Bob Brown moved an amendment requiring the government to enter climate treaty negotiations with an unconditional commitment to reduce emissions by at least 25 per cent below 1990 levels by 2020, and a willingness to reduce by 40 per cent in the context of a global treaty.

speeches.speaker: Alan Ferguson
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme (CPRS), arguing it was environmentally ineffective and economically damaging, with a five per cent emissions target too low and a deal giving $5–6 billion extra to polluters. They highlighted concerns over job losses in the Illawarra (12,000 jobs at risk from BlueScope Steel), electricity price rises of up to 20 per cent, and the need to delay action until after the Copenhagen summit, citing a Galaxy poll showing 54 per cent of Australians supported delay.

speeches.speaker: Christine Milne
speeches.brief: The government's Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme was criticised for redirecting nearly $6 billion from household compensation to coal-fired polluters and for setting emissions targets too weak to avoid catastrophic climate change. The Greens instead advocated for a 40% reduction by 2020 and accused the government of duplicity in locking in coal power.

Senator Bob Brown moved an amendment requiring the government to unconditionally commit to reducing emissions by at least 25% below 1990 levels by 2020, and to express willingness for a 40% reduction in the context of a global treaty.

speeches.speaker: Steve Fielding
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme, arguing it is a multibillion-dollar tax that would harm Australian families and businesses, and demanded a delay until after the Copenhagen climate conference and the US Senate clarifies its position.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government and opposition had stitched up a deal on the Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme without public or expert input, diverting billions of dollars to polluting industries. The speaker also criticised the government for refusing to model a 40 per cent emissions reduction target, despite this being part of the Bali roadmap and recommended by scientists.
